# Vibe Coding Learning Project

A hands-on project to learn **Cursor’s agent customization** : rules, skills, subagents, commands, hooks, and AGENTS.md. Everything is set up with examples and docs so you can try things and tweak them.

## What’s in this repo

**Documentation index:** [docs/README.md](https://github.
com/wchen02/cursor-agent-learning/blob/main/docs/README.md) . **Official Cursor docs (links + how to stay current):** [docs/CURSOR-OFFICIAL-DOCS.md](https://github.com/wchen02/cursor-agent-learning/blob/main/docs/CURSOR-OFFICIAL-DOCS.md) .

## Quick start

1. **Open this folder in Cursor** so it picks up `.cursor/` and `AGENTS.md` .
2. **Read the guide** : [docs/VIBE-CODING-GUIDE.md](https://github.com/wchen02/cursor-agent-learning/blob/main/docs/VIBE-CODING-GUIDE.md) .
3. **Try the examples** :
   
    + Rules and skills: `@general-conventions` , `@typescript-patterns` , `/deploy-checklist` , `/code-review` , `@api-conventions` , `/security-audit` , `/planner` .
    + Subagents: e.g. verifier, debugger (see `.cursor/agents/` ).
    + **Workflows:** Pick a skill from [docs/AGENT-FRAMEWORK-EXAMPLES.md](https://github.com/wchen02/cursor-agent-learning/blob/main/docs/AGENT-FRAMEWORK-EXAMPLES.md) or the themed index [examples/agent-frameworks/README.md](https://github.
com/wchen02/cursor-agent-learning/blob/main/examples/agent-frameworks/README.md) . MCP, hooks, and split-state setup: [docs/ADVANCED-USAGE.md](https://github.com/wchen02/cursor-agent-learning/blob/main/docs/ADVANCED-USAGE.md) , [examples/mcp-servers/README.md](https://github.com/wchen02/cursor-agent-learning/blob/main/examples/mcp-servers/README.md) , `.cursor/hooks/advanced/` .
    + Edit a file and see the example hook behavior (if hooks are enabled).
4. **Do the exercises** : [docs/EXERCISES.md](https://github.com/wchen02/cursor-agent-learning/blob/main/docs/EXERCISES.md) — hands-on tasks for rules, skills, subagents, hooks, and frameworks.
5. **Use the cheat sheet** : [docs/QUICK-REFERENCE.md](https://github.com/wchen02/cursor-agent-learning/blob/main/docs/QUICK-REFERENCE.md) . **Advanced patterns** : [docs/ADVANCED-USAGE.md](https://github.com/wchen02/cursor-agent-learning/blob/main/docs/ADVANCED-USAGE.md) .

## Concepts at a glance
* **Rules** — Short, persistent instructions (style, conventions). Applied by rule type (always / intelligent / file pattern / manual).
* **Skills** — Multi-step workflows. Invoked on demand with `/skill-name` or `@skill-name` .
* **Subagents** — Separate agents with their own context. Good for isolation and parallel work (e.g. verifier, debugger).
* **AGENTS.md** — One markdown file of project instructions; simple alternative to multiple rules.
* **Hooks** — Scripts that run before/after agent actions (e.g. format after edit, audit shell, block risky commands).

See the guide and quick reference for details and examples.

# Cursor scales code retrieval to 1T+ vectors with turbopuffer

Cursor switched from a vector database with a traditional storage architecture to turbopuffer, cutting costs by 20x and unlocking the ability to scale effortlessly as they grow.

95%

cost reduction

1T+

documents

10GB/s

write peaks

80M+

namespaces

turbopuffer is one of the few pieces of infrastructure we haven’t had to worry about as we’ve scaled. Since day one, turbopuffer has felt like they were part of our team.

Sualeh Asif

Sualeh Asif,Co-founder and CTO

##  Why turbopuffer?

turbopuffer’s object storage architecture with unlimited namespaces was a
natural fit for Cursor’s namespace-per-codebase use case. Active codebase
namespaces are loaded into the memory/NVMe cache, and inactive codebase indexes
fade into object storage.

This cold/warm set of tradeoffs was a perfect fit for Cursor

results.title: How Cursor Works Internally? – Aditya Rohilla
excerpts:
If you ask two similar questions back to back, the second one can reuse the vector search results from the first if appropriate, instead of hitting the database again.
* **Memory and Resource Management** – Running heavy models and multiple editor instances can be resource-intensive. The “shadow workspace” feature, for instance, doubles some resource usage (since a hidden VSCode window with language servers is running). Cursor mitigates this by only launching the shadow workspace on demand and tearing it down after some idle time.
* **Extensibility via MCP** – As a forward-looking feature, Cursor supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP). This allows external tools or data sources to be hooked into Cursor’s AI. For example, an MCP plugin could let the AI query your database or fetch documentation from an internal wiki when you ask a question.

In conclusion, Cursor’s engineering marries the capabilities of large language models with the practical tooling of an IDE.

results.title: Inside Cursor 3: The Architecture of an Agent-First IDE in 2026 | by ayush srivastava | Medium
excerpts:
com%2Fplans%3Fdimension%3Dpost_audio_button%26postId%3D60c681a8df1d&operation=register&redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fmedium.com%2F%2540ayush.s0410%2Finside-cursor-3-the-architecture-of-an-agent-first-ide-in-2026-60c681a8df1d&source=---header_actions--60c681a8df1d---------------------post_audio_button------------------)

Share

_From a VS Code fork to a $2B ARR agent orchestration platform — what Cursor actually looks like under the hood today, including Composer 2, the Agents Window, Skills, and everything Cursor 3 changed._

> **_Updated: April 2026_** _| Architecture & Engineering | ~16 min read_
> 
>

When Cursor launched in March 2023, it was a VS Code fork with a clever inline AI suggestion model. By April 2026, it crossed **$2 billion in annual recurring revenue** — doubling in just three months — and shipped Cursor 3, a fundamentally new interface built around agent orchestration rather than file editing.

This article covers the full architecture as it stands today: what has been there since the beginning, and what changed in the explosive 2026 upgrades.
## 📊 By the Numbers (April 2026)

Metric Value Annual Recurring Revenue $2B (Feb 2026) Valuation $29.3B (Series D, Nov 2025) Queries per second 1M+ Parallel agents Up to 8 Fortune 500 adoption ~50% Engineering team ~50 people

## 00 — What Changed from 2025 to 2026

Before diving deep, here’s the delta at a glance:

Area 2025 2026 (Current) Primary UI VS Code IDE with AI panel **Agents Window** (Cursor 3, Apr 2) In-house model Custom Tab model only **Composer 2** (Kimi K2.5 base + Cursor RL) Agent execution Single agent, blocking **8 parallel agents** in isolated Ubuntu VMs Revenue $500M ARR **$2B ARR** Code review Not available **BugBot** — 78% bug resolution rate Self-hosting Cloud-only agents **Self-hosted agents** on your own VPC Other IDEs Cursor-only **JetBrains** integration via Agent Client Protocol Agent knowledge Static Rules only **Skills** — dynamic, on-demand agent capabilities Valuation $9.9B **$29.3B**

## 01 — Foundation: Why Fork VS Code?

...

At roughly **25,000 files and 7 million lines of code** , Cursor is surprisingly compact for its scale. The team of ~50 engineers maintains a pragmatic stack built for speed of iteration:

Layer Technology Role Editor TypeScript + Electron VS Code fork — UI, extensions, keybindings Agents Window TypeScript (scratch) New agent orchestration UI in Cursor 3 Backend TypeScript **monolith** API server, business logic Performance-critical Rust (via Node.js bridge) Indexing, Merkle tree sync, orchestration Agent orchestrator Rust — “Anyrun” Launches isolated VMs via AWS Firecracker Vector store Turbopuffer Embeddings, workspace Merkle trees Docs vectors Pinecone Documentation semantic search Streaming Warpstream (Kafka API) Event data pipeline Auth WorkOS SSO, GitHub / Google login Payments Stripe Subscription & billing

**One intentional choice worth noting:** the backend remains a **monolith** . Cursor’s engineering team consistently chose deployment simplicity over theoretical scalability headroom — and scaled to 1M+ QPS on that monolith with just 50 engineers.

...

**📑 Agent Tabs** View and manage multiple agent conversations side-by-side or in a grid layout. Parallel agents, parallel views.

**🌲 /worktree & /best-of-n** `/worktree` creates an isolated git worktree for a task. `/best-of-n` runs the same task across multiple models in _parallel_ worktrees, then compares outcomes so you can pick the best result.

**🎨 Canvases** Agents generate interactive visual canvases — charts, architecture diagrams, data visualisations — instead of cramming everything into markdown tables.

**📱 Cross-platform agents** Kick off agents from mobile, web, Slack, GitHub, and Linear. All agents appear in the Agents Window regardless of where they were started.

## 06 — Composer 2: Cursor’s New In-House Model (March 19, 2026)

Composer 2 is Cursor’s most significant model investment to date. Unlike the original Tab model (trained purely for speed), Composer 2 is designed for **long, complex agentic tasks** — multi-file edits, multi-step plans, self-correcting loops.

## What makes Composer 2 technically distinctive

...

The model also benchmarks at **4× the generation speed** of comparable frontier models.

> _📝_ **_Note on transparency:_** _The Kimi K2.5 base model was initially not disclosed. An external developer spotted the identifier_ `_kimi-k2p5-rl-0317-s515-fast_` _in system responses. Co-founder Aman Sanger acknowledged the omission and committed to disclosing base models upfront for future releases._
> 
>

## 07 — Skills: Dynamic Agent Knowledge (Cursor 2.4+)

One of the most powerful — and least-known — features in Cursor is **Skills** . Introduced in Cursor 2.4, Skills let you package domain-specific knowledge and workflows that agents can load _on demand_ , rather than cramming everything into always-on Rules.

## Skills vs. Rules — the critical difference

Rules Skills Defined in `.cursor/rules` directory `SKILL.
md` files When loaded **Always** — every conversation **Dynamically** — when agent deems relevant, or you invoke with `/` Best for Coding style, architecture conventions Domain workflows, reusable commands, procedural how-tos Context cost Always uses tokens Only uses tokens when invoked

## What a SKILL.md file can contain

```
# SKILL: API Testing
```

```
## When to use  
Apply when user asks to write or run API tests. ## Commands  
/test-api — Run the test suite against the staging endpoint ## Hooks  
Before running tests: ensure .env.test is loaded  
After running tests: summarize failures in a canvas ## Domain knowledge  
This project uses Vitest, not Jest.  
All API routes require Bearer token auth.  
Mock responses live in /tests/mocks/
```

Skills can include:

* **Custom slash commands** — reusable workflows triggered with `/` in the agent input
* **Hooks** — scripts that run before or after agent actions
* **Domain knowledge** — instructions for specific tasks the agent pulls in on demand

...

* **Memory** — a sidecar model observes sessions and surfaces relevant project context in future conversations
* **Cursor Blame** (Enterprise) — extends git blame with AI attribution, tracking which code came from Tab completions, agent runs (broken down by model), and human edits
* **SOC 2 Type II certified**

## 12 — Scaling to Billions of Completions

The backend data layer handles **over 1 million queries per second** , driven primarily by autocomplete requests fired on each keystroke.

## Database evolution under load

* Started with **YugabyteDB** — migrated away due to sharding complexity
* Moved transactional data to **PostgreSQL**
* Moved vector/embedding storage to **Turbopuffer**
* Completed one critical Turbopuffer migration _during a live outage_ — in hours

## The cold start problem

Parallel agents run in Firecracker microVMs. Cursor maintains a **pool of pre-warmed VMs** to absorb startup latency — applying the serverless warm-pool pattern to agentic workloads.

## 13 — The Three Eras of AI Development

...

│  Tab model · Chat · Composer  2  · BugBot · Canvases      │  
│  Rules (always-on) · Skills (dynamic, SKILL.md)         │  
└────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘  
                         │  
┌────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────┐  
│  INDEXING LAYER                                         │  
│  Merkle tree sync · Vector embeddings · RAG             │  
│  Turbopuffer (embeddings) · Pinecone (docs)             │  
└────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘  
                         │

...

└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Closing Thoughts

What is certain: every major architectural choice — the VS Code fork, the Rust orchestration layer, the in-house Tab model, the Merkle tree sync engine, Skills, and now the Agents Window and Composer 2 — has been in service of a single thesis.

**The editor should disappear. The code should just appear.**

The Tab key was never just a Tab key.

_Sources: Cursor official changelog (cursor.com/changelog), Cursor blog (cursor.com/blog/cursor-3), Cursor best practices (cursor.com/blog/agent-best-practices), The Pragmatic Engineer (June 2025), ByteByteGo (July 2025), NxCode review (March 2026), PopularAITools review (April 2026), igmGuru (April 2026), ServerSpace (April 2026)._

excerpts:
Jörg Schad explains how to tame the complex "data management hairball" to build scalable, safe architectures for AI. He shares how autonomous data products act like containers for data, encapsulating pipelines, schemas, and metadata. Discover how progressive tool discovery via protocols like MCP limits context rot, enforces governance policies, and ensures reliable, multi-modal access.
  
  Autonomous Data Products for the Autonomous Era: Rethinking Data Architecture for GenAI

All in ai-ml-data-eng

Culture & Methods

### Featured in Culture & Methods

* #### Road to Compliance: Will Your Internal Users Hate Your Platform Team?
  
  Davide de Paolis discusses the realities of rolling out cloud infrastructure compliance without fracturing developer relations.

...

Cursor’s [documentation](https://cursor.com/docs/agent/hooks) also provides a simple example: a stop hook that displays a local macOS notification when an agent completes its task. It illustrates how hooks can be used to integrate lightweight automation without needing external services.

Prior to the 1.7 release, developers had been actively requesting this kind of lifecycle control. In one [forum thread](https://forum.cursor.com/t/request-hooks-support-post-edit-pre-edit-etc/114716) , a user wrote:

> ...This would unlock a lot of flexibility for more advanced workflows.
> 
> 

Others proposed use cases such as running tests after edits or tagging AI-authored lines for compliance — features that are now technically possible with Hooks, but not yet widely implemented.

The release of Cursor Hooks has been met with quiet interest but limited visible adoption so far. Cursor’s own [forum discussions](https://forum.cursor.
